title.narrative: Output 7.5. Increased capacity of Member States to develop fair and effective labour migration frameworks, institutions and services to protect migrant workers

description.narrative: The Ministry of Labour (MoL) approved the draft revision of the Ministerial Regulation (MR) on Domestic Workers, under the Labour Protection Act. The MR governs the working conditions for all domestic workers, including migrant domestic workers. The revised version introduces significant improvements including minimum wage, regulated working hours (8-hour workday and 48-hour workweek), and maternity protection (paid leave of 45 days and prohibition of dismissal due to pregnancy) among others. The revision of the regulation started in 2019 and is currently pending approval by the Cabinet and the Counselor of State. In 2022, the Informal Labour Protection Division under the Department of Labour Protection and Welfare (DLPW), MoL, established a committee to review the Ministerial Regulation governing working conditions of agricultural workers to strengthen protection for workers in this sector. This MR covers all workers, including migrant workers. The MoL is exploring the potential to extend, among others, minimum wage and regulated working hours to workers in this sector. In March 2022, MoL revised the Ministerial Regulation on Fisheries Labour Protection B.E 2564. The revisions included an amendment on apprenticeship and the ‘Announcement on Criteria, Method, and Condition of Training on Board a Fishing Vessel in Thai Waters’ which required the standard contract for fishers to be in migrant workers' languages. The apprenticeship changes allow that “The vessel owner or the skipper may have their heir/offspring, a Thai national, aged not less than 16 and certified as an apprentice under the Navigation in Thai Water Law, authorized to be engaged in vocational training in fishing, but not more than one person per vessel". The ILO, with support of the Government of Australia, has continued to advocate for improved protection for domestic workers, including migrant domestic workers, and the revision of the MR on Domestic Workers. This process began in 2019 with the drafting of a gap analysis of the current legal framework vis-à-vis the ILO Domestic Worker’s Convention, 2011 (No 189). Throughout this reporting period, ILO has continued to advocate for a speedy approval of the revised Ministerial Regulation. The ILO, with support of the Government of Australia, has been working with the MoL in their effort to revise the ministerial regulation governing working conditions for workers in the agriculture sector. The process started in Sept 2022, when the DLPW established a working committee to review the MR. ILO has participated in regular meetings since then and continued to advocate for the extension of minimum wage and overtime provisions, regulated working hours, etc. ILO, with support from the European Union, provided technical support to the drafting of the Criteria, Method, and Condition of Training on Board Fishing Vessels in Thai Waters to align with obligations under International Labour Conventions in force in Thailand including C188 (Work in Fishing, C111 (Discrimination (Employment and Occupation) and C 112 (Employment Policy).

title.narrative: 7.5.1. Number of Member States with labour migration frameworks or institutional mechanisms to protect the labour rights of migrant workers and promote coherence with employment, skills, social protection, and other relevant policies
Output 7.5. Increased capacity of Member States to develop fair and effective labour migration frameworks, institutions and services to protect migrant workers

description.narrative: Trade unions and CSO partners supported at least 22,000 migrant workers (50% women) to access services through Migrant Worker Resource Centres (MRCs). At least USD 120,000 compensation was awarded to migrant workers through MRC advocacy. To improve labour inspection, the MOL trained inspectors from the Department of Labour Protection and Welfare (DLPW) and Department of Employment (DoE) officials. This includes 193 DLPW inspectors and 138 DoE officials on ILS, trafficking and forced labour, inspection of domestic work, and violence and harassment; 150 DLPW inspectors trained on ILO forced labour indicators and FL in fishing sectors; and 36 senior inspectors and executives of the DLPW trained on Theory of Change for Labour Inspection in the Thai Fishing and Seafood Processing Sectors. 104 interpreters were trained to better support migrant worker-related investigations. The Ministry of Public Health trained 147 women migrant workers to become certified Migrant Volunteers on Health and Interpretation (MVHIs), who assist in disseminating health information in their communities, provide referrals and conduct outreach activities. The Employers’ Confederation of Thailand (ECOT) developed a guide on ‘Adequate housing for migrant workers in Thailand’ for employers in the construction and agricultural sectors. The Guide provides advice to employers to improve workers’ accommodation with a handy for employers to follow, in adherence to the Workers’ Housing Recommendation (R115). ECOT developed a violence and harassment guide for employers based on ILO guidance to address such issues in the workplace, especially for women migrant workers. The Thai Tuna Industry Association and the Thai Frozen Foods Association agreed to strengthen implementation of the Seafood Good Labour Practices programme to improve living and working conditions in the seafood processing sector. The ILO, with support from the Government of Australia and the EU, built the capacities of CSOs and trade unions to run MRCs. ILO provides resources for staffing and premises, as well as information development and dissemination through outreach. ILO trained interpreters and officers from the DLPW and the DOE to support migrant worker survivors of violence and harassment. Rights-based terminologies were included in training for interpreters, using ILO material. ILO, with support from the EU organized a workshop with DLPW to develop a Theory of Change for improved labour inspections and trained DLPW and MOL officials on forced labour issues. ILO, with support from the EU, supported Raks Thai Foundation (RTF)’s collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health to train MVHIs. ILO supported the development of the ECOT guide through a 2022 study on migrant worker housing in Thailand with recommendations for ECOT, providing technical inputs and supporting consultations with employers. With the support of the EU, ILO trained 79 employers from the construction and agricultural sectors on Thai laws and regulations on workers’ housing and ILO Recommendation 115. ILO, with EU support, trained 133 employers on reducing violence and harassment, 43 construction subcontractors and 8 site managers of the Sansiri construction company on good practices and labour rights. A good practice checklist was developed for inclusion in sub-contractor contracts. ILO, with support from EU, supported an independent assessment of the implementation of the Seafood Good Labour Practices programme in Thailand, with recommendations on how to strengthen it as a voluntary continuous-improvement programme for the seafood industry. Thai Tuna Industry Association and the Thai Frozen Foods Association participated in the assessment. 30 representatives of seafood processing companies and the member companies of Tuna Association of Thailand were trained on fair recruitment.
